draft.title: Isotopes and radioactive decay
card: Isotopes
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. They have the same number of protons, so the same atomic number, but different mass numbers.
Some nuclei are unstable. An unstable nucleus can change by giving off radiation. This is called radioactive decay, and it happens by chance, not because of heat or a chemical reaction.
There are three types of radiation. Alpha particles are a group of two protons and two neutrons. Beta particles are fast electrons. Gamma rays are energy with no particles.
Half-life
the time it takes for half of the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay. After one half-life, half are left. After two half-lives, a quarter are left.
draft.remember: Isotopes differ in neutrons. Unstable nuclei decay, and half-life is the time for half to go.

a.q: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon atoms. What is different about them?
opts: The number of neutrons in the nucleus
The number of protons in the nucleus
The atomic number of the atom
The element that each atom belongs to
a.why: Isotopes of one element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so their mass numbers differ. The number of protons sets the atomic number and the element, so those stay the same.
a.clue: Both are carbon, so one count in the nucleus must be the same.

b.q: A sample of a radioactive isotope has a half-life of 6 hours. Mia starts with 80 g of it. How much of the isotope is left after 12 hours?
opts: 0 g
b.why: 12 hours is two half-lives. After the first, 40 g is left, and after the second, half of that, 20 g, is left. 40 g is the amount after only one half-life, and the sample does not all decay after two.
b.clue: Work out how many half-lives fit into 12 hours.

a.best: The number of neutrons in the nucleus

problems.detail: "Gamma rays are energy with no particles" is loose and slightly misleading. Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic waves with no mass and no charge, and they are carried by photons. Better: "Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic waves with no mass or charge."

check.summary: Both questions are sound, and their intended answers (neutrons; 20 g) are correct. One minor issue: the card's description of gamma rays as "energy with no particles" should say they are electromagnetic waves with no mass or charge.
